command: php tools/external/escpos-php/capture.php character-encodings && node tools/external/escpos-php/capture.js character-encodings
notes: Exercises ESC t codepage switching through its own encoding. The example prints to a FilePrintConnector on php://stdout; the default capability profile names no paper, so the fixture is rendered on the 80 mm paper of the other fixtures. Reviewed as a PNG against what the example prints. The Latin, Greek, Cyrillic and Vietnamese lines all print with their accents, which is the codepage switching working end to end. The half width Katakana line and the Thai line print the fallback box: there is no CJK or Thai font here, as the reference pages say. The Hiragana, full width Katakana, Arabic and Hebrew lines are question marks and boxes in the stream itself, escpos-php could not encode them either. Re-rendered on 2026-09-13, when the katakana codepage gained its glyphs from the second source of tools/generate.js and the glyphs that are wider than the face were fitted into their cell: the diff against the previous golden was reviewed by eye and holds only those two kinds of change, kana where the fallback box stood and a fitted glyph where a clipped left half stood. Re-rendered on 2026-09-14, when the Hebrew and the Thai of the code point set gained their glyphs from the third and the fourth source of tools/generate.js and three rules of the cell were added: a combining mark is centred in its cell by its ink instead of drawn from an origin it sits to the left of, a glyph whose ink lies outside its own advance is fitted by its ink instead of clipped at the edge of the cell, and a Unicode format character is an empty cell whether or not a source has a glyph for it. The diff against the previous golden was reviewed by eye row by row and holds only those changes: a letter where the fallback box stood, a mark where an empty cell stood, and a glyph made whole where a column of it was clipped at the edge of its cell, which here is the Thai ำ and ไ.
